item.title: 2027: SDP candidate promises N200 petrol, free healthcare
item.description: The presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Dr Adewole Adebayo, has promised to reduce petrol prices to N200 per litre without subsidy and provide free healthcare if elected president in 2027. He also pledged free and compulsory education, increased food production, job creation and improved welfare for persons living with disabilities. Adebayo made the promises at an SDP town hall meeting with party leaders, candidates and supporters in Nasarawa State. He urged Nigerians to use the 2027 general election to determine the country’s leadership through the ballot, stressing the importance of electoral participation. Adebayo said the SDP had developed policy proposals to address poverty, unemployment, high living costs and other economic challenges facing the country. On fuel pricing, he said an SDP-led government would reduce petrol prices to N200 per litre without subsidy through improved efficiency and measures to address corruption in the petroleum sector. “We will give you petrol for N200 per litre without subsidy. We will sell it for N200, and NNPC will still make a profit because we will stop funding corruption,” he said. On agriculture, Adebayo said Nasarawa and neighbouring states had the potential to contribute significantly to national food production. “Nasarawa alone can feed Nigeria. Nasarawa, Plateau, Kogi, Kaduna and the Federal Capital Territory have the capacity to feed the whole of Africa,” he said. He also promised free and compulsory education, including measures to expand access to schooling for out-of-school children. According to him, an SDP administration would integrate children in the Almajiri system into formal education while ensuring they continued to receive religious instruction. On healthcare, Adebayo proposed establishing a Federal Medical Centre in every federal constituency and introducing compulsory medical check-ups four times annually. He also promised free medical consultations and medication, although he did not provide details of the proposed funding arrangements. On employment, the SDP candidate pledged to create more job opportunities, including for individuals living with disabilities. He also promised to develop Nasarawa’s mineral resources, including gold, coal, lithium and copper, to promote economic growth and improve the welfare of host communities. Adebayo endorsed the SDP governorship candidate in the state, former Inspector-General of Police, Abubakar Adamu, saying his experience in policing would be an asset in addressing security challenges. He urged voters to assess political candidates based on their records, character and policy proposals rather than party affiliations. The presidential candidate also called for an enabling environment for opposition parties to participate in the electoral process, stressing the importance of political competition in a democracy. Adebayo made the promises at an SDP town hall meeting with party leaders, candidates and supporters in Nasarawa State. Adebayo said the SDP had developed policy proposals to address poverty, unemployment, high living costs and other economic challenges facing the country. On fuel pricing, he said an SDP-led government would reduce petrol prices to N200 per litre without subsidy through improved efficiency and measures to address corruption in the petroleum sector. “We will give you petrol for N200 per litre without subsidy. We will sell it for N200, and NNPC will still make a profit because we will stop funding corruption,” he said. On agriculture, Adebayo said Nasarawa and neighbouring states had the potential to contribute significantly to national food production. “Nasarawa alone can feed Nigeria. Nasarawa, Plateau, Kogi, Kaduna and the Federal Capital Territory have the capacity to feed the whole of Africa,” he said. He also promised free and compulsory education, including measures to expand access to schooling for out-of-school children. According to him, an SDP administration would integrate children in the Almajiri system into formal education while ensuring they continued to receive religious instruction. On healthcare, Adebayo proposed establishing a Federal Medical Centre in every federal constituency and introducing compulsory medical check-ups four times annually. He also promised free medical consultations and medication, although he did not provide details of the proposed funding arrangements. On employment, the SDP candidate pledged to create more job opportunities, including for individuals living with disabilities. He also promised to develop Nasarawa’s mineral resources, including gold, coal, lithium and copper, to promote economic growth and improve the welfare of host communities. Gombe said the town hall meeting provided an opportunity for the party to engage residents, hear their concerns and present its programmes. He urged party members to remain united and participate peacefully in the electoral process. Also speaking, Adamu said the meeting provided an opportunity to interact with residents and understand their expectations of the next state administration. He identified security, justice, accountability and citizens’ welfare as priorities, pledging to incorporate public concerns into government decisions. The meeting was attended by SDP national and state leaders, National Assembly and State House of Assembly candidates, as well as party supporters. item.title: Quantum: 'Five years, that's all we got…'
item.description: SC26 in Chicago had the usual quantum booths, discussions, and hallway optimism. A lot of people were talking about integration with classical HPC and Slurm scheduling for quantum processors, co-design platforms, and GPU-accelerated error correction tools. That part is real and useful. What was harder to find was any result that changed the basic math on when quantum systems will actually do something a supercomputer can't already handle better. I had a long conversation in St. Louis (SC25) with a contact who works deep in quantum and has spent decades in HPC. He's not a skeptic for sport, although that can be fun, sure. Over a grifted free dinner in Chicago (the best kind), his take this year remains the same: the hype keeps outrunning the error rates. Quantum computers generate too many errors to give usable answers on anything interesting. Fixing that is the whole game. And that's a five-year game, minimum. Much like the Bowie anthem in the title. Qubits by the numbers There are two kinds of qubits. Physical qubits are the actual hardware: ions, superconducting circuits, and atoms in a trap. Logical qubits are the ones that do the computation. Each logical qubit is built out of many physical ones so the system can detect and correct errors while it runs. With the traditional surface-code approach, one logical qubit often needs somewhere between 500 and 2,000 physical qubits backing it up, depending on the hardware and the code. One logical qubit by itself is useless. Estimates for basic scientific modeling and small-scale simulation sit in the 100-to-500 logical-qubit range. Take the midpoint of 300. At the low end of the overhead that is 150,000 physical qubits. At the high end it is several million. That is only for early science. Commercial work like molecular mapping for pharma, large optimization problems, complex financial models, pushes into the thousands of logical qubits. National-security and encryption-related work sits even higher. Those numbers have not magically shrunk. A system that can map a modestly sized drug molecule, or run a materials simulation that is still too slow on classical machines, is the kind of workload people actually mean when they talk about useful quantum advantage. Until the logical-qubit counts get there with error rates low enough to finish the job, those problems stay on the machines we already know how to build. Ok, so let's just scale it up This is the world of HPC, we know how to scale stuff, right? Yes, but this isn't a matter of adding a few more racks. Scaling to an additional few hundred thousand physical qubits is not a rack or two or ten. It's probably a dedicated building with its own cryogenics, control electronics, and power draw that is still measured in megawatts even before you get useful logical capacity. item.dc:creator: Dan Olds
item.content:encoded: SC26 in Chicago had the usual quantum booths, discussions, and hallway optimism. A lot of people were talking about integration with classical HPC and Slurm scheduling for quantum processors, co-design platforms, and GPU-accelerated error correction tools. That part is real and useful. What was harder to find was any result that changed the basic math on when quantum systems will actually do something a supercomputer can't already handle better. I had a long conversation in St. Louis (SC25) with a contact who works deep in quantum and has spent decades in HPC. He's not a skeptic for sport, although that can be fun, sure. Over a grifted free dinner in Chicago (the best kind), his take this year remains the same: the hype keeps outrunning the error rates. Quantum computers generate too many errors to give usable answers on anything interesting. Fixing that is the whole game. And that's a five-year game, minimum. Much like the Bowie anthem in the title. Qubits by the numbers There are two kinds of qubits. Physical qubits are the actual hardware: ions, superconducting circuits, and atoms in a trap. Logical qubits are the ones that do the computation. Each logical qubit is built out of many physical ones so the system can detect and correct errors while it runs. With the traditional surface-code approach, one logical qubit often needs somewhere between 500 and 2,000 physical qubits backing it up, depending on the hardware and the code. One logical qubit by itself is useless. Estimates for basic scientific modeling and small-scale simulation sit in the 100-to-500 logical-qubit range. Take the midpoint of 300. At the low end of the overhead that is 150,000 physical qubits. At the high end it is several million. That is only for early science. Commercial work like molecular mapping for pharma, large optimization problems, complex financial models, pushes into the thousands of logical qubits. National-security and encryption-related work sits even higher. Those numbers have not magically shrunk. A system that can map a modestly sized drug molecule, or run a materials simulation that is still too slow on classical machines, is the kind of workload people actually mean when they talk about useful quantum advantage. Until the logical-qubit counts get there with error rates low enough to finish the job, those problems stay on the machines we already know how to build. Ok, so let's just scale it up This is the world of HPC, we know how to scale stuff, right? Yes, but this isn't a matter of adding a few more racks. Scaling to an additional few hundred thousand physical qubits is not a rack or two or ten. It's probably a dedicated building with its own cryogenics, control electronics, and power draw that is still measured in megawatts even before you get useful logical capacity. This is why cutting the massive gap between logical and physical qubits is critical if quantum is going to become even narrowly useful. Signs of (incremental) improvement There is a newer family of codes called quantum low-density parity-check, or QLDPC. In principle they can cut the physical-to-logical ratio substantially — some proposals talk about 10-to-1 or 50-to-1 instead of hundreds-to-one. IBM is building its Starling system, targeted for 2029, around a version of these codes and claims roughly a 10× reduction in overhead compared with surface code for the same logical error rate. That’s progress, assuming it pans out, but it isn’t free. QLDPC needs different hardware connectivity, longer-range couplers, and more sophisticated control and decoding. It is not a drop-in software patch on existing machines. Several groups are working on it, and the first hardware demonstrations are appearing, but no one has yet shown a large-scale system running at those improved ratios on real problems. What we do have are better error rates on small numbers of logical qubits. Quantinuum’s Helios trapped-ion system recently posted a logical memory error rate of about five uncorrectable errors per million rounds — noticeably better than earlier surface-code results from Google. There are also more examples of short algorithms actually running on a handful of logical qubits instead of just memory tests. These are real engineering steps. They do not yet add up to a machine that can run the kinds of calculations people cite when they talk about quantum advantage in chemistry or materials. Current systems are still measured in single-digit to low double-digit logical qubits for anything that looks like an algorithm. At SC26 the clearest quantum signal was that the industry is treating this as an integration problem. IBM, Fermilab, and Nvidia showed work on modular quantum-classical platforms and GPU tools for error correction. Slurm 26.11 [PDF] added support for scheduling quantum resources alongside classical ones. That matters for the people who will eventually have to run these systems inside existing HPC centers. It does not change the qubit math. The practical question for anyone who has to figure out future budgets or power is still the same one my contact laid out in St. Louis: how many physical qubits do you need before you have enough logical ones to do something useful, and when does the hardware actually exist? Roadmaps from the major players still point to the late 2020s for the first fault-tolerant systems that can attempt non-trivial science. Commercial applications sit further out. The error-correction work is moving, the overhead is improving on paper, and the integration with classical systems is real. None of that has moved the bottom line from "still years away" to "ready for production work." Until the logical-qubit counts climb into the hundreds with error rates low enough to finish a real calculation, the interesting problems will keep running on the machines we already know how to build and cool. ®

item.title: Pete Edochie: Linc breaks down in tears as unusual calm rules Enugu residence
item.description: By Benjamin Njoku & By Dennis Agbo Linc Edochie, the third son of the late Pete Edochie, could not hold back his tears when he saw his father’s corpse in the mortuary. The movie legend died in the early hours of Wednesday after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. He had taken ill and was rushed to a hospital in Enugu, where he passed away. Painting a gloomy picture of the atmosphere at the late actor’s riverside residence in Trans-Ekulu, Enugu-based actor and filmmaker, Steve Eboh, said Linc broke down the moment he sighted his father’s body. “When Linc stormed the mortuary and sighted his father’s corpse, he cried profusely and leaned on his brother’s shoulder. We consoled him and prayed for the family,” Eboh said. Eboh added that grief was written all over the faces of people whose lives Pete Edochie had touched during his acting career. “We thank God for a life well spent. He was a legend who touched so many lives. He was not just an actor, he was a global icon. Everybody knew him.” Our correspondent, who visited the late actor’s Trans-Ekulu residence, described a gloomy picture of desertion and sorrow. “Apart from a domestic aide seen at the premises, there was little indication of the tragic development that had thrown the family and the Nigerian entertainment industry into mourning,” he noted. A source familiar with the circumstances surrounding his death told our correspondent that the actor took ill on Tuesday night and was subsequently rushed to a hospital in Enugu, where he died at about 12:30am on Wednesday. According to the source, Edochie’s family had remained at the hospital since his death, apparently attending to necessary arrangements and coming to terms with the loss. The family’s absence from the residence accounted for the quiet atmosphere observed during the reporter’s visit. The post Pete Edochie: Linc breaks down in tears as unusual calm rules Enugu residence appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Why I turned down Burna Boy’s 85/15 demand – Aristokrat boss, Peedi Picasso
item.description: By Benjamin Njoku Peedi Picasso, CEO of Aristokrat Records, has opened up on why he refused to renew Burna Boy’s record deal, saying the singer demanded an 85-15 per cent revenue split in his favour. Picasso, whose real name is Piriye Isokrari said their previous deal gave Burna Boy 60 per cent, while the label took 40 per cent. He also revealed that the singer’s mother insisted he should only sign two-year contracts, a condition that influenced the label’s decision. According to Picasso, the proposed increase did not make financial sense at the time because the label was not making significant money from record sales. Picasso said live performances and endorsement deals were the major sources of revenue. He argued that accepting an 80-20 or 85-15 split would have left the label with a smaller share of the income despite the money it was investing in the singer. Picasso said the arrangement was difficult to justify for another two-year contract, particularly because the label was not entering a long-term deal. However, he admitted that his position has changed, saying he would now accept the terms he previously rejected. “Today I will take the 85/15 per cent now, but back then, it didn’t make any sense,” he said. He also explained that Burna Boy received the larger share of performance earnings under their former agreement because he was the artiste taking the stage. The post Why I turned down Burna Boy’s 85/15 demand – Aristokrat boss, Peedi Picasso appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 8 Sci-Fi Books That Get Even Better the Second Time You Read Them
item.description: Science fiction is a genre built on far-out ideas, strange new worlds, and scientific possibilities that can fundamentally change how we understand our own. Some of the most unforgettable sci-fi novels offer just as much intrigue on a second reading as they do on the first. Whether it's a carefully constructed mystery, an intricate timeline, or a seemingly insignificant detail that takes on entirely new meaning once you know the ending, such books reward readers willing to go back for another speculative look.

item.title: Slow Turnout At Kaduna Polling Unit As INEC Holds Mock Accreditation
item.description: There is a slow turnout at polling units 031 and 032 in Ungwan Boro, Sabon Tasha ward, in Chikun Local Government Area of Kaduna State, as there is little to suggest that the mock accreditation exercise set to hold today by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is taking place. As at the time of filing this report, at exactly 9:29 am , officials of the Independent National Electoral Commission were yet to be on ground to commence the exercise scheduled to commence by 8:3am. The only security presence observed is that of three personnel of the Nigeria Security CIVIL Defence Corps (NSCDC) There is also no presence of voters at the two polling units, raising questions about the level of preparedness and awareness ahead of the exercise. The situation contrasts with INEC’s earlier assurance of readiness for the mock election, which is designed to assess its operational capacity and the effectiveness of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and result transmission technology ahead of the 2027 general elections. As at Friday night, when voting materials were distributed at the INEC office in Kaduna, the Administrative Secretary, Abba Yahaya, also assured the public of the Commission’s readiness for the mock election, expressing confidence in its preparedness to conduct the exercise. The exercise is expected to simulate the 2027 Presidential election, with polling units opening by 8:30 a.m. and accreditation running from 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. The situation is, however, slightly different at polling unit 002, located within Narayi Primary School, also in Chikun Local Government Area. As of 10 a.m., some voters were seen hanging around the polling area, awaiting the commencement of the exercise. However, as at the time of this report, INEC officials were yet to arrive, leaving the voters waiting without any indication of when the mock election would begin. The post Slow Turnout At Kaduna Polling Unit As INEC Holds Mock Accreditation appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: Lawal pledges more projects as APC Campaign visits Shinkafi
item.description: Governor seeks support for Tinubu, APC candidates ahead of 2027 polls Zamfara State Governor, Dauda Lawal, has pledged to execute more development projects in Shinkafi Local Government Area as he canvassed support for the All Progressives Congress (APC) ahead of the 2027 general elections. Lawal made the pledge on Friday during the APC Zamfara North campaign flag-off rally held at the Eid ground in Shinkafi. The rally attracted party chieftains, including the Director-General of the Tinubu/Shettima Presidential Campaign Council and former governor, Abdul’aziz Yari; another former governor, Mahmuda Aliyu Shinkafi; the state APC Chairman, Kabiru Moyi; and other party leaders. Tens of thousands of supporters reportedly welcomed the campaign entourage at the town’s entrance, chanting slogans in support of the party. Addressing the gathering, Lawal thanked the people of Shinkafi for their solidarity and warm reception, saying their support was encouraging. He said his administration had recorded achievements in education, healthcare, infrastructure and economic development. The governor disclosed that his administration had rehabilitated six primary healthcare centres, including facilities in Badarawa, Birnin Yero, Galadi, Jangeru and Kurya. He described the ongoing referral hospital project in Shinkafi as a legacy initiative that would transform healthcare delivery in Zamfara State and the North-West. According to him, the project is central to his administration’s commitment to improving access to quality healthcare. Lawal also said his administration had completed 22 of the 31 projects undertaken over the past three and a half years, while the remaining nine were at more than 80 per cent completion. He urged residents to support President Bola Tinubu, his administration and other APC candidates in the 2027 general elections. “I am here once again to seek your votes. Vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, vote for me, and vote for the APC from top to bottom in the upcoming 2027 general election,” he said. The governor’s spokesman, Sulaiman Bala Idris, disclosed this in a statement issued on November 27, 2026. The post Lawal pledges more projects as APC Campaign visits Shinkafi appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Chelsea in a ‘difficult moment’ admits Alonso
item.description: Xabi Alonso admitted Chelsea are in a “difficult moment” as the beleaguered boss urged his struggling side to stick together after their dismal 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest on Friday. Alonso’s side crashed to a third successive Premier League loss to leave them languishing in eighth place. The Blues have lost four of their last five league matches, piling pressure on Alonso just months into his reign at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea fell behind to Igor Jesus’s early opener before Morgan Gibbs-White doubled Forest’s lead with a second half penalty. Emmanuel Emegha reduced the deficit but Gibbs-White struck again to make Emega’s late second nothing more than a footnote on another dispiriting evening for Alonso. “It’s a difficult moment for everyone. It’s disappointing again to lose again but we need to keep trying to find solutions, we can’t stop,” Alonso said. “We are low in confidence, the team is struggling to hold a result. After getting to 2-1 we have conceded and go to 3-1. “Everything is not going our way, we are responsible for that and we are responsible to find solutions.” Chelsea have already conceded 23 goals in 12 league matches and their porous defence was not helped by Alonso’s curious decision to use Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo in a back-three. Alonso also selected Wesley Fofana after the centre-back was forced to apologise for joking in a YouTube interview about missing a penalty during Chelsea’s League Cup defeat against Liverpool this season. The hapless Fofana was booed by angry Chelsea fans at the City Ground and conceded a penalty with his careless foul on former Blues striker Liam Delap. “We need to support everyone. Everyone that is in the team we need to support,” Alonso said of Fofana. “We know we have to go through difficult moments. We don’t take apart anyone and we want to help.” Asked to assess Chelsea’s dismal run, Alonso suggested the only cure was hard work on the training ground. “We can do better for sure. At this level you need to hold results and that is why we are losing in the last games,” he said after Chelsea’s sixth league defeat his term. “That is the only way I understand football. When things are not going well, try to work and find solutions. It can happen that we turn it around and it goes our way.” Chelsea’s sixth league defeat under Alonso will spark pointed questions about the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss. Although Alonso led Leverkusen to an historic Bundesliga title in 2024, he lasted just seven months before being sacked by Real. The former Liverpool midfielder desperately needs a win against bottom of the table Crystal Palace on Wednesday to avoid the sack talk growing even louder. “Everyone needs to stick together and go through this moment. We have to deal with it,” he said. The post Chelsea in a ‘difficult moment’ admits Alonso appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Unkernel and Trynix just transported computing to 2035
item.description: What's the difference between just-for-fun demo hacks, and serious carefully designed large-scale software architecture? It's the quick-and-dirty jobs that end up transforming computing. A blog post earlier this week called 2035 came early led the Reg FOSS desk down what we thought was a fascinating, and possibly quite scary, rabbit-hole… but it turned out to be an entire warren. We thought we were still in 2026, but in turns out that in some ways, tech just leaped forward a decade. To try to convey the point of this blog post – why what had been just a fun clever little hack has the potential to take half a century of OS and hypervisor design and throw it out of the nearest window – will take quite a lot of unpacking. If you bear with us, we will try to walk you through it. To get started, we need to go back a decade or more. Stick with this: there are laughs, as well as hammers taken to beloved ideas. The year of 2035 and the ideas around that come from a remarkable talk by Gary Bernhardt of Destroy All Software, which is both funny and highly educational. It will really massively assist understanding what this article and the technology is all about if you have the time to watch the talks. The Reg FOSS desk is not at all fond of spoken-word video as a medium – we much prefer to read than listen – but the three talks we're going to mention are golden, among the very best presentations this century in all of computing and IT. Seriously, they are worth your time. As a preface, before we go into Bernhardt's half-hour information-dense talk, let's warm up with a four-minute funny one. But first, let's look at the context for that. Step 0: JavaScript is the language of web programming In 2009, Jeff Atwood laid this out in an article called All Programming is Web Programming . It's still coming true today. Software is getting very blurred around the edges. The entire SaaS industry means that massive organizations run on web apps. Tech like Electron embeds a web browser inside JavaScript apps built in Node.js, while Progressive Web Apps make websites look like local program windows. The most popular desktop Linux in the world is ChromeOS Flex, which doesn't support local native applications at all. Everything is browser windows, even the desktop. It's all built in JavaScript. And yet… Step 1: JavaScript is kind of weird and kind of bad. Bernhardt made this case in 2012, with a celebrated lightning talk called Wat , from the CodeMash conference in 2012. Wat walks through a whole list of examples of how JavaScript is a very strange programming language and does very strange things that are not at all what you might expect. Some of the jokes will make more sense to programmers, but we reckon anyone who has ever fought with a recalcitrant bit of software will get some laughs from it – and that probably applies to all readers of The Register. Step 2: JavaScript is in the process of conquering the world. Bernhardt moved on to much bigger ideas at PyCon 2014

item.content:encoded: What's the difference between just-for-fun demo hacks, and serious carefully designed large-scale software architecture? It's the quick-and-dirty jobs that end up transforming computing. A blog post earlier this week called 2035 came early led the Reg FOSS desk down what we thought was a fascinating, and possibly quite scary, rabbit-hole… but it turned out to be an entire warren. We thought we were still in 2026, but in turns out that in some ways, tech just leaped forward a decade. To try to convey the point of this blog post – why what had been just a fun clever little hack has the potential to take half a century of OS and hypervisor design and throw it out of the nearest window – will take quite a lot of unpacking. If you bear with us, we will try to walk you through it. To get started, we need to go back a decade or more. Stick with this: there are laughs, as well as hammers taken to beloved ideas. The year of 2035 and the ideas around that come from a remarkable talk by Gary Bernhardt of Destroy All Software, which is both funny and highly educational. It will really massively assist understanding what this article and the technology is all about if you have the time to watch the talks. The Reg FOSS desk is not at all fond of spoken-word video as a medium – we much prefer to read than listen – but the three talks we're going to mention are golden, among the very best presentations this century in all of computing and IT. Seriously, they are worth your time. As a preface, before we go into Bernhardt's half-hour information-dense talk, let's warm up with a four-minute funny one. But first, let's look at the context for that. Step 0: JavaScript is the language of web programming In 2009, Jeff Atwood laid this out in an article called All Programming is Web Programming . It's still coming true today. Software is getting very blurred around the edges. The entire SaaS industry means that massive organizations run on web apps. Tech like Electron embeds a web browser inside JavaScript apps built in Node.js, while Progressive Web Apps make websites look like local program windows. The most popular desktop Linux in the world is ChromeOS Flex, which doesn't support local native applications at all. Everything is browser windows, even the desktop. It's all built in JavaScript. And yet… Step 1: JavaScript is kind of weird and kind of bad. Bernhardt made this case in 2012, with a celebrated lightning talk called Wat , from the CodeMash conference in 2012. Wat walks through a whole list of examples of how JavaScript is a very strange programming language and does very strange things that are not at all what you might expect. Some of the jokes will make more sense to programmers, but we reckon anyone who has ever fought with a recalcitrant bit of software will get some laughs from it – and that probably applies to all readers of The Register. Step 2: JavaScript is in the process of conquering the world. Bernhardt moved on to much bigger ideas at PyCon 2014, in a much deeper talk called The Birth & Death of JavaScript . We do recommend that you watch it – you can right-click the video and speed playback up if you wish – but first, some context. This talk is not what it seems. This is a talk delivered in 2014, which as we write is 12 years ago. However, the talk purports to be a historical one, given in 2035, looking back at how software developed over the last 20 years. As you read this, 2035 is nearly a decade in our future… but the conceit of the talk is that it's looking back from 21 years ahead. 2014 was quite a while ago. It's the year Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 disappeared, and following Ukraine's Maidan revolution, Russia invaded Crimea . So the perspective of Bernhardt's fanciful talk is the history of the period 2014 to 2035. The talk makes some crazy predictions about the spread of JavaScript – which by 2035 is a near-forgotten historical artifact, which Bernhardt emphasizes by consistently mispronouncing its name. Currently, in 2026, we are about half way there, chronologically speaking – but one of the surprising aspects is that quite a lot of the tech predictions in the talk have already come true. This 2014 talk already looking eerily predictive. Saying that, the talk says it takes place after some unspecified global disaster, which might be World War 3 or something else. That's looking not improbable, too. The talk says that because JavaScript is both bad, and wildly popular, it enabled Asm.js – enabling compilers for any language to target browsers' Javascript runtimes. In 2015, Asm.js evolved into Wasm, which is very real. When The Register introduced Wasm, our title almost paid homage to Bernhardt's – we referred to JavaScript creator Eich's latest project: KILL JAVASCRIPT . Step 3: Wasm replaces JavaScript, ending all platform rivalries By 2022, as we reported, Wasm was able to support LibreOffice. A few years later, we got a demo of this working as a web page plugin. Wasm is here, it's surprisingly fast, and it turns some of Bernhardt's talk into reality: it dispenses with the actual programming language-level part of JavaScript, and turns it into the mother of all cross-platform runtimes. Which brings us to the practical upshot, and how Bernhardt's predictions continue to come true. LibreOffice is bigger than the Linux kernel now. If you can run a gigabyte of LibreOffice in a web page with just a few seconds' interruption, then it is no problem to run a whole-system emulator. The Internet Archive uses this to run vintage games, and as we reported in 2022 , the former MacOS9.app site used emulation to boot and run real old versions of classic MacOS in the browser. That has now turned into Infinite Mac, and it's no longer limited to Classic MacOS: today, it can run NeXTstep, early development versions of what became Mac OS X, and as of last month it even runs BeOS . The more perceptive reader may have already foreseen where this is going. Step 4: Wasm replaces containers and hypervisors On November 15th, Iranian developer Pooya Parsa announced his Unkernel project on X . By November 19th, he published v0.2. (As given away by the lengthy README on its Github, it's LLM-assisted.) Unkernel boots a real Linux kernel inside a Arm64 runtime, written in Zig and compiled to Wasm. When you visit the Unkernel.dev page, it boots Debian 13, on a real Linux kernel, running inside your browser tab. It has 2 GB of RAM and two virtual CPU cores. It has a very simple GUI, using Wayland; press Super+K for the app launcher. Which means that, yes, you can run Doom on it. This is one of the core technological predictions of Bernhardt's talk, 12 years ago. Why bother with a hypervisor when you can just compile to Wasm and boot the identical binaries on anything – Arm, x86, RISC-V, whatever. "Run what ya brung," as the drag-racing fraternity says. Bernhardt predicted that by the end of the 2020s, everyone would target a platform he called METAL: what's now called Wasm, right in the OS kernel – rather than targeting old-fashioned 20th century operating systems. Well, now that developers have access to LLMs to speed up the tedious "writing code" stage of implementation, that enables them to turn fever dreams into reality faster than ever. In his post 2035 came early, Farid Zakaria introduces Trynix. Rather than running Debian on the Unkernel, it runs NixOS instead, with all of the vast Nix multiverse of nearly a third of a million programs and versions. It has Wayland, supports OpenGL and ALSA sound, so it can run GUI and media software. And on FOSS desk's 15-year-old iMac, it runs Doom. On a slightly newer machine, we successfully launched Firefox on Linux, inside Chrome on Linux. True, Doom is not an immensely useful application for this technology, but another example is Michael Lohr's SideBySide . A single browser tap contains three parallel panes, containing Firefox, Chromium, and the WebKit-based Epiphany. Enter a URL and it opens

item.title: Basque to the future: Andoni Iraola fired up for first Merseyside derby
item.description: Liverpool head coach sees parallels with Athletic v Sociedad derby as he comes up against his old foe David Moyes “I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape. “It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.” Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings
item.description: Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue Restaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them. This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf. Continue reading...

The exit of Arsenal manager, Renée Slegers, 18 months after delivering European glory was somewhat inevitable, her position made untenable after six home draws in six games and just 15 points from 11 games, but will it solve the Gunners’ problems? item.title: CHINA DIARIES: Where Students Build the Future
item.description: I must confess, I was not quite prepared for what I saw during my visit to the Qinling Workshop at Xi’an Aeronautical Vocational and Technical College in China. For someone fascinated by technology and innovation, walking into the institution’s aircraft hangar was an experience in itself. There were aircraft and helicopters, aviation equipment and specialised training facilities. For a moment, it felt less like visiting a school and more like stepping into an aviation engineering centre. But the biggest surprise was yet to come. Beyond the aircraft and helicopters, I encountered something that left an even stronger impression: drones designed, developed and assembled by students. China Diaries: The Railway Connecting Continents China Diaries: The future of farming These were not simply classroom models or academic projects put together to earn grades. The students were experimenting with different drone technologies, exploring their applications and developing solutions to practical problems. There were different designs and innovations, reflecting the creativity, technical confidence and curiosity of young people who were not waiting until graduation to start making a contribution to society. It was exciting to see. One could immediately imagine the possibilities: drones that could help farmers monitor crops and spray farmlands, support environmental monitoring, conduct aerial surveys, inspect infrastructure and assist emergency response operations. What struck me most was the philosophy behind what I was seeing. Technology was not being taught as an abstract subject. Students were being encouraged to understand problems and develop technological solutions. An institution built around practical skills The Qinling Workshop visit offered an opportunity to appreciate the work of Xi’an Aeronautical Vocational and Technical College, an institution with a strong focus on aviation, engineering and technical education. Its programmes cover a wide range of disciplines, including aviation manufacturing, aircraft maintenance, aircraft engine technology, drone application technology, general aviation, mechanical engineering, artificial intelligence, computer technology, robotics, automation, electronic information, aviation logistics and automotive technology. Students also study specialised areas such as CNC machining, intelligent manufacturing, aircraft electronic systems, materials engineering, welding technology, surveying and remote sensing, software development, big data, airport operations and civil aviation services. The breadth of these programmes is significant. It shows an understanding that an aviation and manufacturing economy requires much more than pilots and aircraft engineers. item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Shehu
item.content:encoded: I must confess, I was not quite prepared for what I saw during my visit to the Qinling Workshop at Xi’an Aeronautical Vocational and Technical College in China. For someone fascinated by technology and innovation, walking into the institution’s aircraft hangar was an experience in itself. There were aircraft and helicopters, aviation equipment and specialised training facilities. For a moment, it felt less like visiting a school and more like stepping into an aviation engineering centre. But the biggest surprise was yet to come. Beyond the aircraft and helicopters, I encountered something that left an even stronger impression: drones designed, developed and assembled by students. China Diaries: The Railway Connecting Continents China Diaries: The future of farming These were not simply classroom models or academic projects put together to earn grades. The students were experimenting with different drone technologies, exploring their applications and developing solutions to practical problems. There were different designs and innovations, reflecting the creativity, technical confidence and curiosity of young people who were not waiting until graduation to start making a contribution to society. It was exciting to see. One could immediately imagine the possibilities: drones that could help farmers monitor crops and spray farmlands, support environmental monitoring, conduct aerial surveys, inspect infrastructure and assist emergency response operations. What struck me most was the philosophy behind what I was seeing. Technology was not being taught as an abstract subject. Students were being encouraged to understand problems and develop technological solutions. An institution built around practical skills The Qinling Workshop visit offered an opportunity to appreciate the work of Xi’an Aeronautical Vocational and Technical College, an institution with a strong focus on aviation, engineering and technical education. Its programmes cover a wide range of disciplines, including aviation manufacturing, aircraft maintenance, aircraft engine technology, drone application technology, general aviation, mechanical engineering, artificial intelligence, computer technology, robotics, automation, electronic information, aviation logistics and automotive technology. Students also study specialised areas such as CNC machining, intelligent manufacturing, aircraft electronic systems, materials engineering, welding technology, surveying and remote sensing, software development, big data, airport operations and civil aviation services. The breadth of these programmes is significant. It shows an understanding that an aviation and manufacturing economy requires much more than pilots and aircraft engineers. It needs technicians, software developers, mechanics, materials specialists, electronics experts, maintenance professionals and people who can design, manufacture and repair equipment. The institution has developed specialised workshops, laboratories and practical training facilities to support this approach. What makes the model particularly interesting is the government’s involvement in supporting vocational education. The college operates within China’s publicly supported technical education system, with government funding and student support arrangements helping to make technical training more accessible. I was particularly interested in learning about the tuition subsidies available to students. This is an important development consideration. Technical education requires expensive equipment, specialised instructors and facilities that many students and families may struggle to afford without institutional and government support. China’s investment in this area reflects an understanding that producing skilled technicians is not simply an educational responsibility. It is also an economic and industrial priority. Investing in China’s young people One thing I noticed was that the student population was predominantly Chinese, with relatively few international students. This is significant because it shows that the institution’s primary focus is developing the technical skills of China’s own young population. The young people I encountered were being equipped with practical knowledge that could feed directly into the country’s aviation, manufacturing, technology and industrial sectors. There is an important lesson here for developing countries. Education should not only prepare young people to search for jobs. It should also equip them with the capacity to create products, provide services, solve problems and contribute to economic growth. A country that wants to industrialise needs more than university graduates. It needs a large pool of technically competent people who understand how things work and, more importantly, how to make them work. The drones I saw were a practical illustration of this thinking. A student who can design and assemble a drone, programme its flight systems and identify its possible applications is acquiring skills that can be translated into economic opportunities. What Nigeria can learn My visit inevitably brought Nigeria to mind. We have universities, polytechnics, colleges of technology and technical schools offering courses in engineering, agriculture, computer science and related disciplines. We also have young people with enormous creative potential. But there is a need to strengthen the connection between what students learn in classrooms and the practical demands of the economy. Imagine a Nigerian polytechnic where agricultural technology students work with engineering and computer science students to develop drones for farmers. Imagine students designing affordable machinery for small-scale manufacturers, developing solar-powered equipment for rural communities or creating digital solutions for transportation and healthcare. These are not unrealistic ambitions. They are possibilities that can emerge when education is properly connected to innovation. There are several areas where our institutions can learn from this experience. First, we need to invest more deliberately in practical training facilities. Engineering students should have access to functioning laboratories, workshops, machinery and opportunities to develop prototypes. A student studying drone technology, for instance, should have opportunities to design, assemble, programme and test drones. Second, we need stronger partnerships between educational institutions and industry. Companies should participate in curriculum development, provide equipment, offer internships and give students real problems to solve. Third, we should encourage multidisciplinary innovation. A drone project may require expertise in electronics, software engineering, mechanical engineering, artificial intelligence, geography and agriculture. Bringing students from different disciplines together can produce solutions that would otherwise be difficult to achieve. Fourth, government support for technical education deserves greater attention. If we want more young Nigerians to acquire specialised skills, we must make vocational and technical training affordable and accessible. This requires investment in facilities, scholarships, tuition support, instructors and industry partnerships. An opportunity for Nigeria-China cooperation There is also an opportunity to take this relationship beyond trade and infrastructure into education and technology transfer. Nigeria and China could explore partnerships between technical institutions, including student and faculty exchanges, joint research, scholarships, specialised training and the development of practical training centres. Our institutions could benefit from Chinese expertise in aviation maintenance, drone technology, robotics, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and automation. International cooperation should, however, go beyond sending a few students abroad to acquire certificates. We should explore arran

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 28 – Apollo 17 VIP Site Anaglyph
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 28 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Apollo 17 VIP Site Anaglyph Explanation: Get out your red/blue glasses and check out this stereo scene from Taurus-Littrow valley on the Moon! The color anaglyph features a detailed 3D view of Apollo 17’s Lunar Rover in the foreground. Behind it lies the Lunar Module and distant lunar hills. Because the world was going to be able to watch the Lunar Module’s ascent stage liftoff via the rover’s TV camera, this parking place was also known as the VIP Site. Fifty years ago , in December of 1972, Apollo 17 astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt spent about 75 hours on the Moon, while colleague Ronald Evans orbited overhead . The crew returned with 110 kilograms of rock and soil samples, more than from any of the other lunar landing sites. Cernan and Schmitt are still the last to walk ( or drive ) on the Moon . item.title: 7 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Food
item.description: Anything can be the star of a Far Side comic . While most of them featured stupid humans or talking animals as their main characters, the surrealist streak in cartoonist Gary Larson sometimes gave life to inanimate objects as well. For example, there’s a strip where a jogger tells a living pair of scissors that they can no longer run together. And if scissors can be alive in The Far Side comics, just about anything can, including food.

item.title: USWNT seal Women’s World Cup qualification with 8-0 win over El Salvador
item.description: US goes up 7-0 over El Salvador by half-time Win secures spot at 2027 World Cup and 2028 Olympics The United States’ place at a Women’s World Cup is treated as a foregone conclusion, but Friday’s all-or-nothing qualifier against El Salvador gave some reason for nerves. This was the first competitive game for Emma Hayes’ team since their Olympic gold medal match in August 2024, the end of two years of only friendlies. Given the global advances in women’s soccer over the years, maybe El Salvador could spring an all-time upset. The suspense ultimately lasted for eight minutes and 20 seconds. The USWNT opened the scoring in their Concacaf W Championship quarter-final with El Salvador in the ninth minute; a nifty training-ground set piece routine ending with Kennedy Wesley prodding the ball into the net, putting the hosts in the driver’s seat for an 8-0 win and a spot in next summer’s big show. With the win, the US maintains their perfect Women’s World Cup attendance record, a part of all 10 tournaments to date. Continue reading...

item.title: 8 Classic PlayStation Games That Are Barely Playable Today
item.description: If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

item.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
item.description: The M5-powered MacBook Air is $300 off in both size configurations for Black Friday. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June , you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199. Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5) Where to Buy: $1299 $999 at Amazon (512GB) $1299 $999 at Best Buy (512GB) $1599 $1199 at Amazon (1TB) Apple MacBook Air 15 (M5) Where to Buy: $1299 $1199 at Amazon (512GB) $1299 $1199 at Best Buy (512GB) $1799 $1499 at Amazon (1TB) The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount , is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls. Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model , the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display , or one of the M6-powered machines . A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable. Read our M5-powered MacBook Air review .

item.title: The absolute best Black Friday deals you can still get
item.description: Black Friday is nearly over, but many of this year’s best deals are still available. You can still find some of the lowest prices we’ve seen in-store and online for video games , wireless earbuds , TVs , robot vacuums , and so much more. We can’t guarantee a deal you’ve had your eye on will last through Cyber Monday; however, if prior years are any indication, most will stick around through the long weekend. As usual, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge . With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. item.title: 63 Years Later, CBS's Legendary 70-Episode Series Still Has the Only Vampire Worth Watching
item.description: It’s Fangsgiving here at Polygon, our Thanksgiving celebration of stories about fanged creatures of all types and especially vampires . I didn't want to be left out, but, to be honest, I always thought vampires were kind of dumb. They're a horror movie staple, but they’re rarely all that scary. There’s usually a romantic element to their stories that I also find tiresome . Perhaps I’ve just never seen the right vampire movies, but overall I find vampires to be pretty lame.

item.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
item.description: Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW's ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023 , China's BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity. It's called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase. According … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
item.description: The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has hit a new low price just a few months after release. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Black Friday is entering the evening, which means one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch is coming to a close. After all, the holiday savings can help offset the unfortunate price hikes from earlier this year, when Apple raised the cost of some of its most popular gear. Some discounts still apply to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro , too, which are available at their lowest prices to date. In addition to a variety of discounts across retailers, Apple is offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases between November 27th and November 30th. How much you get back is determined by how much you spend, with up to $100 available for some iPhone and Apple Watch purchases, and up to $300 for the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That said, in some cases you may be able to save more by buying from other retailers. Earbud and headphone deals AirPods Pro 3 The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review. Where to Buy: $249 $149 at Amazon $249 $149 at Walmart $249 $149.99 at Best Buy Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review. Where to Buy: $249 $179.95 at Amazon $249 $179.95 at Walmart $249.99 $179.99 at Best Buy You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review . The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon and Best Buy , which is $19 shy of their best price to date ( Target also has them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review . Beats Studio Pro The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review . Where to Buy: $349.99 $139.95 at Amazon (select colors) $349.99

The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review . The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,749 ($250 off) at Amazon and Best Buy , which is a new low price. The Pro builds on its predecessor with a faster chip and support for Wi-Fi 7. In our testing, it handled multitasking, photo editing, and occasional video editing with ease while still delivering exceptional battery life. It lacks the newer MacBook Pro’s gorgeous OLED display, but its Mini LED screen still looks great, especially given its smooth 120Hz refresh rate. It also offers excellent speakers and a good selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SD card slot. Read our review . It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review . Where to Buy: $399 $299 at Amazon (GPS, 42mm) $399 $329 at Best Buy (GPS, 42mm) $449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm) The Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration starting at $179 ($50 off) at Amazon and Walmart , matching its best price to date, while Best Buy is currently $20 higher. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. Read our review . AirTags, chargers, and other deals Apple AirTag (second-gen) Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review. It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batterie

item.title: The best robot vacuums we’ve tested are up to 60 percent off for Black Friday
item.description: The Eufy Omni C28 has dropped to a new low of $379.99 for Black Friday. | Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge Black Friday is here, and if you want a little help keeping your floors clean this holiday season, now is a great time to pick up a robot vacuum. Some of the best models we’ve tested over the last year or two are on sale for up to 60 percent off, whether you’re after a basic robovac for quick cleanups or a more advanced model that vacuums, mops, and practically takes care of itself. This year’s sale has made some pricier robot vacuums a lot more affordable. The Eufy Omni C28 , for example, now costs about what you’d expect to pay for a budget bot, while the Matic — which impressed us with its almost humanlike navigation — is getting a rare discount in the form of a bundle. If none of those are quite what you’re looking for, we’ve also found good deals on models from Roborock , Dreame, and more, with picks below for a variety of budgets and cleaning needs. Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review . Where to Buy: $999.99 $549.99 at Amazon $999.99 $549.99 at Roborock Roborock Q10 S5 Plus Despite lacking a multifunction dock, the budget-friendly robot vacuum and mop offers an impressive set of features for the price, including AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, automatic mop lifting, and a self-emptying dock. Where to Buy: $549.99 $229.99 at Amazon $549.99 $229.99 at Roborock Matic robot vacuum The Matic robot vacuum and mop is ideal for cluttered homes with pets, multiple floors, and a mixture of carpets and hardwood. It offers almost humanlike navigation, tackling high-pile rugs and mopping up wet spills. The quiet bot also requires less maintenance than many rivals thanks to its onboard water tank and dust bag. Read our review. Where to Buy: $1795 $1395 at Matic (Standard Bundle) $1995 $1595 at Matic (Serene Bundle) Eufy Omni C28 The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors. Where to Buy: $799.99 $379.99 at Amazon $799.99 $379.99 at Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1) Dreame X60 Ultra The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets. Where to Buy: $1499.99 $999.99 at Amazon $1499.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (with Dreame W10 vacuum) $1499.99 $999.99 at Dreame Narwal Flow 2 The Narwal Flow 2 is an excellent robot vacuum for hardwood floors. Where to Buy: $1499.99 $749 at Amazon $1499.99 $749 at Best Buy Switchbot K11 Plus The Matter-compatible SwitchBot K11 Plus is ideal for small apartments, bedrooms, and home offices. Where to Buy: $399.99 $169.56 at Amazon (with on-page coupon) $399.99 $160 at SwitchBot (with code BFCMX60) Dreame X50 Ultra With high suction power, an improved brush system, and the ability to scale thresholds up to 6cm, the X50 Ultra stands out as a great robot vacuum-mop hybrid. While its 20,000Pa suction isn’t quite as powerful as the X60 Ultra’s and it can’t tackle especially high thresholds as well, it’s still an excellent option. Its edge cleaning also isn’t quite as effective as the X60 Ultra’s, but you’re otherwise getting many of the same features for a lot less. Where to Buy: $1599.99 $799.99 at Amazon $1599.99 $799.99 at Dreame $1599.99 $799.99 at Target Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2 The Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2 delivers powerful 25,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a self-cleaning dock that empties the dustbin, washes the mop, and refills its water tanks. Unlike the X50 Ultra, however, it lacks the ability to climb high thresholds or stairs. Where to Buy: $799.99 $474.98 at Amazon Narwal Freo X Ultra The Freo X Ultra features spinning triangular mop pads and can swing slightly to reach baseboards. Its large charging dock holds two big water tanks, while Narwal’s disposable onboard bin compresses the dust. It’s also relatively quiet when it returns to the dock, and its anti-tangle brush and 8,200Pa of suction perform well on most carpets. Where to Buy: $699.99 $399.99 at Amazon

item.title: Sony’s 1000XM4C headphones are a Black Friday bargain at $198
item.description: The fan-favorite folding design returns with the comfortable, slightly improved XM4C headphones. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon , Best Buy , and Walmart . That’s $100 off their October launch price. Sony WH-1000XM4C Where to Buy: $299.99 $198 at Amazon $299.99 $198 at Walmart $299.99 $199.99 at Best Buy There’s a reason why Sony went back to refine the XM4. Our former reviewer Chris Welch praised them for being super comfortable and for having close to perfect features for the price, especially compared to its successor, the XM3 (still my daily driver, for what it’s worth). The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up. These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027. Read our Sony WH-1000XM4C review .

item.title: Yooka-Laylee’s free upgrade is skipping Xbox
item.description: Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition | Image: Playtronic Games Playtronic Games is getting ready to launch Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition as a free update on PlayStation 5, Switch 2, and PC on December 15th. Unfortunately for Xbox owners, the developer says it "can't commit to any additional platforms for the foreseeable future." In a statement posted on X , Playtronic said that it understands the frustration some players may feel, but that bringing the Definitive Edition to Xbox just isn't viable "given the technological challenges and costs," and reminded people that they're a small team. item.title: Many of our favorite Blu-ray movies are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
item.description: Blade Runner 2049 looks fantastic, even if you pick up the 1080p Blu-ray version. | Image: Alcon Entertainment No shade to those who love their subscription services, but viewing physical movies is a time-honored tradition that shouldn’t go away. Watching them doesn’t feel all that different, but deciding which movie to watch feels less annoying; sifting through a movie collection on your shelf or in a storage binder is so much more fun (and less overwhelming) than scrolling endlessly in apps. While standard Blu-ray players that display movies at up to 1080p are fairly inexpensive, 4K Blu-ray counterparts that can show movies in all their 4K HDR glory are significantly pricier (but totally worth it if you’re a movie buff). No matter the player you own, there are always Blu-ray deals, and the discounts are especially good during Black Friday. We’ve highlighted some of our favorites below, though Amazon, Barnes & Noble, and Gruv are each overflowing with more deals than we could realistically wedge into our coverage. KPop Demon Hunters The once-Netflix-exclusive animated film is now available on 4K Blu-ray at a great price. Where to Buy: $49.95 $24.98 at Amazon (4K + Blu-ray) $49.95 $39.96 at Criterion (4K + Blu-ray) $49.95 $24.99 at Barnes & Noble (4K + Blu-ray) High and Low Akira Kurosawa’s High and Low showcases how capitalism can rot our moral compasses. Where to Buy: $49.95 $24.98 at Amazon (4K + Blu-ray) $49.95 $39.96 at Criterion (4K + Blu-ray) $49.99 $24.99 at Barnes & Noble (4K + Blu-ray) Sinners Ryan Coogler’s Sinners delivers a memorable plot with some fantastic mid-movie dance choreography. This movie’s part of Gruv’s “3 for $33” sale. Where to Buy: $34.98 $24.99 at Gruv (4K Blu-ray + code) Star Trek: The Next Generation Own the complete run of The Next Generation across 41 discs in 1080p resolution, currently the most hi-res option available. Where to Buy: $179.99 $134.99 at Amazon (Blu-ray) $179.99 $134.99 at Best Buy (Blu-ray) The Lord of the Rings Trilogy One of the best Black Friday deals, bar none. The set includes the theatrical cuts of the trilogy, plus the extended editions. Where to Buy: $67.8 $49.49 at Amazon (4K Blu-ray) The Matrix: 4-Film Déjà Vu Collection Setting aside that not every Matrix movie is amazing, the Déjà Vu set includes them all for less than if you bought them separately. Where to Buy: $84.99 $34.99 at Amazon (4K + Blu-ray) $84.99 $44.99 at Walmart (4K + Blu-ray) The Princess Bride One of Rob Reiner’s many classics, but the only one with a truly fantastic, feisty line read from Mandy Patinkin. item.title: Arteta sets Arsenal 100-point Premier League target to emulate Manchester City
item.description: ‘It’s only been done once and that’s what we want’ Arteta not being drawn on City’s financial charges Mikel Arteta has set Arsenal the ­target of emulating Manchester City by becoming only the second team in Premier League history to record 100 points in a season. Arteta was an assistant for Pep Guardiola’s side when they achieved the landmark in the 2017-18 campaign, beating second-placed Manchester United by 19 points. City head to the Emirates Stadium on Sunday already trailing Arsenal by six points after just 11 games, with Enzo Maresca’s side having failed to win any of their four previous league matches. Continue reading...

The Italian’s first game as the club’s manager came at the Stadium of Light in April and relegation was on the cards when his new side slipped to a 1-0 defeat . Survival was secured on the final day of last season but he is taking nothing for granted after a promising run of form. Continue reading...

item.title: Spygate tensions erupt at Southampton after Finn Azaz’s cry-baby celebration riles Boro
item.description: When asked whether he had any regrets about running the length of the pitch to goad the Middlesbrough supporters he used to call his own with a mock crying celebration, Finn Azaz was unequivocal. “None whatsoever,” said the Southampton playmaker. And you get the sense that very few associated with his club disagreed. Southampton, and their manager Tonda Eckert, long ago admitted their Spygate crime. Based on the behaviour of many connected to the south-coast club – their manager a notable exception – they have embraced it. The sense of aggrievement that it cost them the chance of promotion last season remains. Continue reading...

item.title: Gibbs-White and Igor Jesus fire Nottingham Forest past shaky Chelsea
item.description: Wesley Fofana, as a former Leicester player, might have expected the celebrating Nottingham Forest fans to give him a hard time. But, at the end of a week in which he invited opprobrium by making light of missing a penalty at Liverpool in an unsanctioned French interview, he endured the ultimate ignominy when Chelsea supporters followed a four-letter suggestion to tell the defender: “You’re not welcome here.” Fofana was humiliated by Liam Delap before fouling the former Chelsea striker for a penalty that Morgan Gibbs-White converted for the first of his two goals. The result, coming after Forest’s win against Manchester City in their last match at the City Ground, means they climb three points clear of the Premier League’s relegation zone. Continue reading...

item.title: From Asake to Darkoo: 5 New Nigerian & African Music Videos to Watch This Weekend
item.description: Zlatan, Peruzzi, and Shoday from the official visuals for their collaborative single “Inferno.” Photo Credit: Peruzzi/Instagram Between Friday traffic in Lagos, Sunday afternoon wind-downs, and the official countdown to Detty December already kicking into gear across Nigeria, the final weekend of November arrives with a stacked line-up of fresh visuals worth queuing up on your screen. From street-hop swagger and a ninth-anniversary gospel love note by one of Nollywood and Afrobeats’ favourite couples to a pan-African dancefloor link-up between Benin and Tanzania, these five music videos deliver plenty to replay all weekend long. Skilful – Asake Lifted from his chart-topping 2026 album M$NEY, Asake brings his unmistakable log-drum bounce and choir-backed street-hop cadence to the official visual for “Skilful”. Built around his nimble Yoruba wordplay and self-assured reflections on hard-earned success, the record moves at an upbeat, club-ready tempo made for late-night drives and weekend speakers. On screen, Mr. Money leans straight into high-fashion street theatrics, pairing bold styling with fast-paced choreography and tight framing that keeps your eyes locked on every beat drop. “On My Way” – Susu x Banky W. You may have noticed Adesua Etomi-Wellington—performing here as Susu—kept an unusually low profile for much of 2026, and the backstory behind her new duet with Banky W. puts every lyric into focus. Behind the scenes, she spent months navigating back-to-back hospital visits, scans, tests, and medical procedures across Nigeria and the United States—a gruelling season she summed up simply: she is not easily broken. Released to celebrate nine years of marriage and serve as the lead single from their forthcoming 2027 album Not Easily Broken, “On My Way” turns that survival story into a joyful Afro-gospel and R&B thanksgiving record. Watching the two of them sing and dance together on screen hits differently once you know what they walked through this year—it is warm, unguarded, and the kind of visual that lifts your whole mood on a quiet Sunday morning. Kakua – Angélique Kidjo feat. Diamond Platnumz Five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo teams up with Tanzanian Bongo Flava giant Diamond Platnumz on “Kakua”, a vibrant cross-continental collaboration linking West and East Africa. Driven by brisk percussion, bright brass accents, and call-and-response hooks sung across French, Yoruba, and Swahili, the track carries an immediate, celebratory pulse from its opening bars. The accompanying visuals match the song’s global spirit with vivid colour palettes, kinetic dance sequences, and celebratory styling that turns every frame into a pan-African street party. Inferno – Peruzzi, Zlatan and Shoday You have probably been listening to “Inferno” non-stop already, jamming to it on playlists, in traffic, and everywhere speakers are turned up—and now the official video takes that same madness to another level. Peruzzi sets the pace with his effortless, hook-hea

item.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo
item.description: First, Uganda is heading for the exit in eastern DR Congo. Kampala has announced the withdrawal of its troops from a key town in North Kivu, as relations with Kinshasa deteriorate following provocative comments from Uganda's army chief. Then, pregnant women are struggling to cope with extreme heat, while health experts warn of growing risks for unborn babies, from dehydration to premature births. And, after seeking safety, opportunity and a better life, many migrants in South Africa now face hostility, violence and growing exclusion. As anti-immigration sentiment gains ground, the country's promise is fading for those who once saw it as a land of hope.
