item.title: Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions After Winning CAS Appeal
item.description: Idrissa Gana Gueye and captain Sadio Mané hold the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations trophy, which the Court of Arbitration for Sport confirmed belongs to Senegal after setting aside CAF’s Appeal Board decision. The months-long off-pitch dispute surrounding the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) final has come to an official close, with Senegal reinstated as the tournament’s champions. Today, Tuesday, 24 November 2026, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) —the independent international body headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, that settles global sports disputes through arbitration—ruled unanimously in favour of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) . The verdict overturns the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Appeal Board’s earlier decision that stripped the Teranga Lions of the trophy and handed a 3–0 forfeit victory to hosts Morocco. For football lovers across the continent, many of whom watched two of Africa’s finest sides battle through one of the most dramatic finals in AFCON history, the verdict restores the outcome decided on the pitch in Rabat on 18 January 2026. In that January final at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Senegal edged Morocco 1–0 after extra time courtesy of a decisive strike from Pape Gueye . However, the match had been halted late in regulation time while still goalless after referee Jean – Jacques Ngambo Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty following a VAR review. Several Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest for roughly 14 minutes before returning—following interventions from teammates including captain Sadio Mané —to finish the match in the 109th minute (90+19). Morocco’s Brahim Díaz missed the resulting penalty, and Senegal went on to win in extra time. Senegal celebrate their 2025 Africa Cup of Nations triumph in Rabat—a title officially restored on 24 November 2026 after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned CAF’s forfeiture ruling. Two months later, in March 2026, CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal’s temporary walk-off amounted to a forfeiture under Articles 82 and 84 of the competition regulations, awarding Morocco a 3–0 administrative win and the championship. The FSF lodged its appeal with CAS on 25 March 2026, followed by a closed-door hearing in Lausanne on 8 October 2026 before a three-member panel presided over by French sports law expert Prof. Gérald Simon , alongside Prof. Luigi Fumagalli (Italy) and Prof. Dr. Ulrich Haas (Germany). In its official statement released today, CAS confirmed that Senegal’s original victory stands: “The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025). The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at

The months-long off-pitch dispute surrounding the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) final has come to an official close, with Senegal reinstated as the tournament’s champions. Today, Tuesday, 24 November 2026, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) —the independent international body headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, that settles global sports disputes through arbitration—ruled unanimously in favour of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) . The verdict overturns the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Appeal Board’s earlier decision that stripped the Teranga Lions of the trophy and handed a 3–0 forfeit victory to hosts Morocco. For football lovers across the continent, many of whom watched two of Africa’s finest sides battle through one of the most dramatic finals in AFCON history, the verdict restores the outcome decided on the pitch in Rabat on 18 January 2026. In that January final at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Senegal edged Morocco 1–0 after extra time courtesy of a decisive strike from Pape Gueye . However, the match had been halted late in regulation time while still goalless after referee Jean – Jacques Ngambo Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty following a VAR review. Several Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest for roughly 14 minutes before returning—following interventions from teammates including captain Sadio Mané —to finish the match in the 109th minute (90+19). Morocco’s Brahim Díaz missed the resulting penalty, and Senegal went on to win in extra time. Senegal celebrate their 2025 Africa Cup of Nations triumph in Rabat—a title officially restored on 24 November 2026 after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned CAF’s forfeiture ruling. Two months later, in March 2026, CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal’s temporary walk-off amounted to a forfeiture under Articles 82 and 84 of the competition regulations, awarding Morocco a 3–0 administrative win and the championship. The FSF lodged its appeal with CAS on 25 March 2026, followed by a closed-door hearing in Lausanne on 8 October 2026 before a three-member panel presided over by French sports law expert Prof. Gérald Simon , alongside Prof. Luigi Fumagalli (Italy) and Prof. Dr. Ulrich Haas (Germany). In its official statement released today, CAS confirmed that Senegal’s original victory stands: “The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025). The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 fo r Senegal).” Explaining its reasoning, the panel noted that the referee’s decision to restart play fell squarely within his sole authority and was protected by football’s “field of play” doctrine, meaning it could not be overturned retrospectively. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume,” CAS stated. “In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.” Senegal captain Sadio Mané celebrates on his teammates’ shoulders with the 2025 AFCON trophy, officially restored to the Teranga Lions after CAS ruled in favour of the Senegalese Football Federation. The panel also rejected arguments from the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) that the referee had acted arbitrarily or erred in law, adding that Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations apply only when a match is permanently abandoned—not when play resumes and concludes. “The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension,” the statement added. “However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as ‘arbitrary’. On the contrary, the Referee’s judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.” CAS further noted that separate disciplinary sanctions had already been handed down by CAF to the FSF, head coach Pape Thiaw , and certain players over the walk-off incident. With the ruling now official, Senegal retain their second AFCON title, bringing a decisive close to one of the biggest off-pitch sagas in modern African football. *** Photo Credit: Sadio Mané/Instagram The post Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions After Winning CAS Appeal appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: YunLone Galaxy star projector review — a sub-$30 customizable night light
item.description: null The YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom. Costing around $28, this star projector can display beautiful dancing auroras across your walls and ceiling, and thanks to app support, a huge range of color options are available. In fact, the color combinations you can display here are almost infinite. Key specs Size: 3.54 x 3.15 x 4.72 inches (9 x 8 x 12 cm) Weight: 17.6 ounces (500 g) Bulb Type: LED Laser: Yes Operation: App and remote control Rotation: Yes Sleep timer: Yes Speaker: Yes With built-in sounds, a Bluetooth speaker and endless customization options, this really is an all-singing, all-dancing star projector. We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic. This isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector . But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Design The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith Solid build quality Functional rather than aesthetic design Limited buttons on the front of the unit The YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light . You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however. That isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. Given the wide reach of the projector, it helps spread the aurora lights across your entire room. The projector has a solid build quality: It's plastic but feels sturdy and well-made. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. Those rubber feet help prevent it from being knocked off a desk or bedside table, too. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Performance Projections produced by the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. Kim Snaith Projections produced by the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. item.dc:creator: Kim Snaith
item.content:encoded: null The YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom. Costing around $28, this star projector can display beautiful dancing auroras across your walls and ceiling, and thanks to app support, a huge range of color options are available. In fact, the color combinations you can display here are almost infinite. Key specs Size: 3.54 x 3.15 x 4.72 inches (9 x 8 x 12 cm) Weight: 17.6 ounces (500 g) Bulb Type: LED Laser: Yes Operation: App and remote control Rotation: Yes Sleep timer: Yes Speaker: Yes With built-in sounds, a Bluetooth speaker and endless customization options, this really is an all-singing, all-dancing star projector. We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic. This isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector . But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Design The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith The Yunlone Galaxy Projector has a simple but effective design. Kim Snaith Solid build quality Functional rather than aesthetic design Limited buttons on the front of the unit The YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light . You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however. That isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. Given the wide reach of the projector, it helps spread the aurora lights across your entire room. The projector has a solid build quality: It's plastic but feels sturdy and well-made. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. Those rubber feet help prevent it from being knocked off a desk or bedside table, too. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Performance Projections produced by the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. Kim Snaith Projections produced by the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. Kim Snaith Colorful projections Great customizability via the app Wide-reaching projector As already mentioned, the YunLone Galaxy Projector isn't a scientific star projector. If you want to recreate actual constellations and close-ups of planets on your bedroom ceiling, this is not the projector for you. But if you're looking for beautiful, mesmerizing aurora-style patterns, it's a great choice. Once you're connected to the app, you can control exactly what colors the projector displays. Not only can you choose from a number of preset arrangements — labeled as seasons, colors or holidays, so you can create a mood that matches the time of year or how you feel — but you can set your own entire color scheme by choosing from a color wheel. You can also set the brightness, whether the lights will have a "breathing" effect, and how fast they ripple across your ceiling. It's a very neat touch, and it goes beyond what we'd expect to find in a star projector in this price range. If you don't want to bother with app connection, you can still set a range of colors and options from the remote control, but the options here are more limited. A projection produced by the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. (Image credit: Kim Snaith) The YunLone Galaxy Projector comes equipped with a laser, so it can project green laser stars onto your walls and ceiling. We didn't love the look of these, though, so it's good that you can turn them off independently of the aurora lights. You can also change the laser's brightness if you'd like the stars to appear dimmer. Both the laser stars and the aurora projections have a very wide reach, covering most of the walls and ceiling of the bedroom we tested the unit in. Obviously, this will vary depending on the size of your room and how far away from the ceiling/wall you place the unit, but we were pleasantly surprised by the coverage offered by this projector. YunLone Galaxy Projector: Functionality Speaker with preset sounds and Bluetooth Remote control App functionality The YunLone Galaxy Projector has a companion app that can be downloaded onto an Android or Apple smartphone. Once the app is set up and paired with your unit, you have full control over the colors, speed and brightness of your projections. The pairing process isn't entirely straightforward, however, with no simple way of forcing the projector to enter pairing mode. The instructions tell you to quickly turn the unit on and off three times, but it took several attempts before we successfully put the projector into pairing mode. The YunLone Galaxy Projector's on-body buttons and remote control. Kim Snaith Thankfully, once that's done, it should stay paired with your smartphone permanently so you won't have to repeat the process. And the app itself is very easy to use, working seamlessly to change the colors of the projection unit. The bundled remote control (which requires two AAA batteries, not included) is a little more complex than most, offering a range of buttons to control both the built-in speaker and the light itself. We'd highly recommend opting for the app option as it gives you much better control over the unit, but if your smartphone is unavailable, you can at least set basic color and speed with the remote. You can connect a music player to the projector via Bluetooth to play your own audio through its built-in speaker. The quality is decent rather than outstanding: It obviously doesn't match the sound of a specialist speaker, but it's as good as we'd expect any $28 speaker to be. It lacks the bass that music requires to sound "complete" but will be ideal for listening to audiobooks and podcasts. In a neat touch, the YunLone Galaxy Projector also has eight built-in sound effects, including white noise, waves, lullabies and a storm, which some users may find relaxing and good to fall asleep to. The remote control unit for the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. Kim snaith The app of the Yunlone Galaxy Projector. Kim Snaith Should I buy the YunLone Galaxy Projector? We have been thoroughly impressed with what the YunLone Galaxy Projector offers. Its projections are beautiful auroras that dance across your ceiling, and the ability to fully customize the color and speed is something that we really didn't expect to find at a $28 price point. If you're on a budget and looking for a non-scientific projector to use to relax and unwind with, we really don't think you can find a better unit. If, however, you want something that offers more scientific projections, you'll need to look elsewhere. Sega Toys' range of projectors, including the Homestar Flux and the Homestar Classic , is excellent but comes with a much bigger price tag. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector is worth considering too, offering realistic projections but with a price tag closer to $50. The good thing about these projectors is that they come with interchangeable discs, able to display various images of space. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector has several discs in the box, but you'll need to buy extra discs for the Sega Toys range, so that’s an extra cost to factor in.

item.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
item.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

item.title: Olam Agri Rewards Loyal Dealers at Customer Awards & Recognition Night
item.description: Olam Agri ’s wheat milling and pasta business, Crown Flour Mill ( CFM ) Limited, honoured its top customers, dealers and distributors at its Customer Awards & Recognition Night, marking more than 15 years of partnership. Held under the theme “Celebrating Partnerships, Rewarding Excellence,” the event brought together company leadership and long-standing partners from Northern, Eastern and Western Nigeria. It paid tribute to the distributors who built markets and the dealers who remained committed through shifting economic conditions. Their enterprise and confidence have carried CFM’s products to customers and communities across the country. The highlight of the evening was the rewarding of CFM’s best-performing dealers across three categories: Trailblazer, Sterling and Titan. Winners received 5-tonne, 10-tonne and 15-tonne trucks, as well as baking ovens. The night closed with the presentation of a 45-tonne truck to the overall best-performing dealer. L-R: Charles Babarimisa, Head of Sales; Siddharth Suri, Vice President/Business Head; Nitin Mehta, Managing Director, all of Crown Flour Mill (CFM) Limited; and Alhaji Oluwasesan Sose, the overall best-performing distributor and winner of a 45-tonne truck, during the presentation of award prizes. Nitin Mehta, Business Head, Wheat Milling & Pasta Business, Olam Agri, said the milestone reflects far more than time. “Fifteen years of growing together represents relationships built on trust, shared ambition and resilience. Our dealers and distributors have helped us extend our market reach, serve customers better and strengthen our position in the industry. Through changing market dynamics and different challenges, the strength of our partnerships has been a constant source of resilience.” Sanusi Modinat (5th from right), a dealer, with her award and the key to a 15-tonne truck, her reward for her performance. Bolaji Anifowose , Vice President & Commercial, Olam Agri, described dealers as strategic partners rather than an extension of the distribution network. “Their market knowledge, entrepreneurial drive and commitment connect our brands to consumers across the country. Our focus now is on strengthening these partnerships, improving market reach, enhancing distribution efficiency and creating more opportunities for our partners to grow. A stronger dealer network means a stronger business.” The overall best-performing dealer, Alhaji Oluwaseun Sose, called the award a proud moment. “My relationship with the company has been built on trust, consistency and a shared commitment to growth. It has been a journey of learning, overcoming challenges and identifying opportunities together. This recognition encourages me to keep striving for excellence.” The runner-up, Opeyemi Sanusi Modinat, praised the company’s collaborative approach. “Our partnership has given us opportunities to grow, expand our market presence and serve more customers. What makes it special is the understanding that our success matters too.

item.title: Inside the 2026 WISCAR Mentoring Walk
item.description: Mentors, mentees, professionals and members of the public gathered at Eko Atlantic, Lagos, on Saturday, November 14, 2026, for the annual Women in Successful Careers (WISCAR) Mentoring Walk . Led by WISCAR Founder and Chairperson, Amina Oyagbola , the walk forms part of the lead-up to the organisation’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference. Participants were paired up for the walk along the Eko Atlantic, each with someone they had not met before. At the end of the route, they switched to new mentor-mentee partners for a short mentoring session, which gave everyone two fresh conversations in one morning. Back at the meeting point, participants shared what they had learnt from their partners, from career advice to personal lessons. Nutritionist Sherese Ijewere then led a session on healthy eating and answered questions on everyday food choices. Coach Bobbie Tee of Happy Heart Fitness, closed the morning with a Zumba session. Next stop: the conference The walk sets the stage for WISCAR’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference , themed “ Courage in Action: Shaping Policies and Structures for Inclusive Progress. ” The conference takes place on Saturday, November 28, 2026, at the Civic Centre, Lagos. Highlights include: A keynote from Dr Ndidi Nwuneli , former President and CEO of the ONE Campaign and Founder of LEAP Africa, who will also receive this year’s Distinguished WISCAR Award. Speakers including Badejo-Okusanya , SAN, President of the Nigerian Bar Association, and Mallam Ahmed Ladan Gobir, President of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) The launch of WISCAR’s CIPM-endorsed Corporate Mentoring Playbook The graduation of Cohort 2 of the Women in Law Mentoring Programme Register now at https://wiscar.ng/almc . Sponsored Content The post Inside the 2026 WISCAR Mentoring Walk appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
item.description: Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view. Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geostrategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race. item.title: China launches Pakistani astronaut to Tiangong space station, its 1st international visitor, alongside Shenzhou-24 crew (video)
item.description: null China launched an international astronaut, Pakistan's first space traveler to reach orbit, to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong space station , a three-module orbital lab that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) item.content:encoded: null China launched an international astronaut, Pakistan's first space traveler to reach orbit, to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program. A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong space station , a three-module orbital lab that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) The Chinese Manned Space Engineering (Image credit: VCG/VCG via Getty Images) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. The six astronauts of China's Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 crews give thumb's up signs in blue jumpsuits on the Tiangong Space Station. (Image credit: CMSE) Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Pakistan's first orbital astronaut, pilot Mohammed Zishan Ali (left), salutes alongside Shenzhou-24 crewmates Tang Hongbo (center) and Wu Yi before their launch into orbit. (Image credit: Xu Xun/VCG via Getty Images) Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

item.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
item.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

item.title: Watch November's full Beaver Moon live online today with supermoon livestream
item.description: null Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. November's full moon rises tonight (Nov. 24)! You can see live telescopic views of the "Beaver supermoon" courtesy of the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP). The free YouTube livestream begins at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) and will feature live views of the moon captured by a suite of robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. Today's stream features expert commentary from VTP founder Gianluca Masi, along with photos of previous full moons shining above historic landmarks in the heart of Rome. What makes the November full moon special? November's full moon is often called the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the industrious animals are hard at work building dams and preparing for the winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . It is also set to be a spectacular supermoon , which reaches peak illumination while within 90% of perigee — the closest point to Earth in the moon's 27-day elliptical orbit. You might like: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon . Supermoons can be up to 13% larger and 30% brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, which occurred in May earlier this year as the natural satellite shone opposite the sun in Earth's sky while close to apogee, when it is farthest from our planet. Interested in capturing your own mesmerizing views of the full moon? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the lunar disk , along with our roundups of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography . Editor's Note: If you would like to share your photos of the Beaver Moon with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), along with your name, location and thoughts to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Nigeria and Tanzania to Co-Host Inaugural WHAS in Abuja, Mobilising Continental Action for Better Women’s Health
item.description: The Governments of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the United Republic of Tanzania will jointly host the inaugural Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Held under the theme “Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health,” WHAS 2026 will convene approximately 300 senior decision-makers, including Heads of State, First Ladies, Ministers of Health and Finance, African Union (AU) leadership, development finance institutions, philanthropists, and health innovators, to move Africa from political commitment to accountable investment and delivery. As a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform, WHAS is designed to advance women’s health across the entire life course, encompassing maternal, reproductive, and gynaecological health, noncommunicable diseases, and menopause, by treating women’s health not merely as a social priority, but as a central driver of Africa’s economic and social progress. Investing in women’s health is also an investment in Africa’s productivity, economic resilience, and future prosperity. WHAS 2026 bridges the flagship African Union Champion mandates of the two co-hosting nations. Serving as founding convener, Nigeria brings the political leadership and health workforce agenda championed by His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, AU Champion for Human Resources for Health and Community Health Delivery Partnership. Nationally, WHAS is anchored in the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , with presidential facilitation by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health (OSSAP-WH) . As co-host, Tanzania brings its continental leadership on maternal and child health, championed by Her Excellency, President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, advancing the Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026–2030 and its Three Zeros: Zero Home Delivery, Zero Preventable Maternal and Newborn Deaths, and Zero Unvaccinated Children. Tanzania’s co-hosting is delivered through the Ministry of Health, led by Hon. Mohamed Omary Mchengerwa , Minister of Health, and the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health. item.content:encoded: The Governments of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the United Republic of Tanzania will jointly host the inaugural Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 on Tuesday, 1 December 2026, at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM. Held under the theme “Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health,” WHAS 2026 will convene approximately 300 senior decision-makers, including Heads of State, First Ladies, Ministers of Health and Finance, African Union (AU) leadership, development finance institutions, philanthropists, and health innovators, to move Africa from political commitment to accountable investment and delivery. As a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform, WHAS is designed to advance women’s health across the entire life course, encompassing maternal, reproductive, and gynaecological health, noncommunicable diseases, and menopause, by treating women’s health not merely as a social priority, but as a central driver of Africa’s economic and social progress. Investing in women’s health is also an investment in Africa’s productivity, economic resilience, and future prosperity. WHAS 2026 bridges the flagship African Union Champion mandates of the two co-hosting nations. Serving as founding convener, Nigeria brings the political leadership and health workforce agenda championed by His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, AU Champion for Human Resources for Health and Community Health Delivery Partnership. Nationally, WHAS is anchored in the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , with presidential facilitation by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health (OSSAP-WH) . As co-host, Tanzania brings its continental leadership on maternal and child health, championed by Her Excellency, President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, advancing the Continental Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026–2030 and its Three Zeros: Zero Home Delivery, Zero Preventable Maternal and Newborn Deaths, and Zero Unvaccinated Children. Tanzania’s co-hosting is delivered through the Ministry of Health, led by Hon. Mohamed Omary Mchengerwa , Minister of Health, and the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health. Speaking ahead of WHAS 2026, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, CON , Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, described the Summit as an important platform for advancing collaboration, shared learning, and African ownership of the women’s health agenda: “ The Women’s Health Africa Summit is a great platform for bringing together leaders, advocates, practitioners, academics and financiers to identify gaps, mobilise action and facilitate shared learning across countries. Indeed, women’s health is a global issue, and even wealthier countries continue to face significant gaps in this area. Ultimately, responsibility lies with us as leaders on the continent. We must take ownership of our health priorities.” Echoing the commitment to continental solidarity and measurable progress, Hon. Ummy Ally Mwalimu , Special Adviser to the President of the United Republic of Tanzania on Maternal and Child Health and Head of the Secretariat of the African Union Champion for Maternal and Child Health, highlighted the synergy between both nations’ leadership agendas: “Under the leadership of Her Excellency President Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, AU Champion for Maternal and Child Health, Tanzania is proud to co-host WHAS with Nigeria. Collaboration between our two AU Champions is an implementation imperative, not simply a matter of institutional goodwill. Coordinated leadership is essential to align workforce investment, community health delivery, sustainable financing and accountability with country-led priorities, avoid fragmented efforts and translate continental commitments into measurable results. The Three Zeros of the Continental RMNCAH Roadmap depend on competent, adequately supported frontline health workers, functional referral systems and effective community outreach. WHAS, under the theme ‘Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health’, provides a timely platform for these shared commitments.” Pathfinder International , serving as Lead Technical Partner, is supporting programme design, technical content, strategic partnerships, and efforts to connect political leadership, financing, and country-led implementation, including practical follow-up beyond the Summit. Highlighting the broader vision of WHAS, Dr. Adanna Steinacker , Senior Special Assistant to the President on Women’s Health, noted: “ For too long, women’s health has been treated as a secondary concern or viewed narrowly through a single stage of life. WHAS changes that paradigm, bringing African governments, capital, and innovators together to back women’s health across the entire life course as a core pillar of our continent’s social and economic future.” Structured around three enduring pillars: Innovation, Financing, and Delivery , WHAS 2026 will focus on strengthening the frontline and specialist health workforce required to deliver quality care to women and girls at every stage of life. WHAS will seek to secure an initial set of country and institutional commitments, including accelerated action on neglected gynaecological conditions, while establishing an enduring framework for African-led collaboration and post-summit accountability. Event : Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) 2026 Date : Tuesday, 1 December 2026 Time : 12:00 PM – 7:00 PM WAT Venue : State House Banquet Hall, Abuja, Nigeria Theme : Health Workforce for Better Women’s Health Co-Hosts : Federal Republic of Nigeria and United Republic of Tanzania Lead Technical Partner : Pathfinder International Related milestones : Joint Roadmap Dialogue, Addis Ababa, 24 November 2026; Political and Delivery Dialogue at WHAS, Abuja, 1 December 2026 For more information and partnerships, visit womenshealthafricasummit.com . About the Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) The Women’s Health Africa Summit (WHAS) is a Nigeria-led, African-owned continental platform dedicated to advancing women’s health across the life course. Built on the three pillars of Innovation, Financing, and Delivery, WHAS brings together governments, political leaders, financing institutions, innovators, and delivery partners to strengthen health systems, mobilise domestic and international capital, and accelerate equitable access to quality healthcare for women across Africa. item.title: How Williams Alamu Graduated with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan
item.description: Williams Alamu marks his B.Sc. First-Class Honours graduation in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. There was a time when Williams Alamu would rather not sit an examination than risk getting a grade he wasn’t happy with. A B or a C in his Cambridge A-levels felt like a possibility he wasn’t ready to entertain, so he didn’t write the exams. A few years later, at 23, he has graduated from the University of Ibadan with a B.Sc. in Statistics, First-Class Honours and a CGPA of 3.65/4.0. Somewhere along the way, he decided that fear was no longer going to make his decisions for him. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. There were 5:30am wake-ups, difficult Statistics courses, friends who became unofficial tutors, a ChatGPT Pro subscription in 300 level, job offers he turned down and one Demography exam that kept him awake for 36 hours. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. Williams Alamu seated in a University of Ibadan lecture hall before a test during his Statistics degree. When I eventually gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I didn’t want to repeat that experience. I saw university as an opportunity to approach things differently. When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. Williams Alamu seated in a University of Ibadan lecture hall before a test during his Statistics degree. When I eventually gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I didn’t want to repeat that experience. I saw university as an opportunity to approach things differently. Rather than allow the fear of falling short to determine what I attempted, I wanted to embrace the challenge and give it my best effort. That’s where the ambition to become the Best Graduating Student in my faculty came from. In the end, I didn’t graduate as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty or department, but I graduated with a First Class, and that’s something I’m genuinely happy about. It wasn’t exactly the outcome I had envisioned, but unlike my experience with Cambridge A-levels, I didn’t allow the fear of falling short to stop me from trying. I set a goal, gave it my best effort, and saw it through. For me, that alone was a significant part of my growth. Explain your systems. Beyond “reading hard,” what were the specific study techniques or daily schedules that kept you at the top? I think one of the most important things I did was try my best not to miss classes. I attended a public university, so there were always distractions, but I made a conscious effort to be present. I wouldn’t say I paid 100% attention in every class, but I realised there was value in simply being there. Sometimes, lecturers made important statements or gave hints that proved useful in examinations. I also started studying by the fourth week of each semester, after giving myself some time to settle in and enjoy school. I would go over what had been taught that week and revisit earlier topics whenever I needed more background knowledge. Whenever I struggled with a question or finally understood a difficult concept, I took notes so I could return to them during examinations rather than start figuring things out all over again. Handwritten probability and mathematical Statistics notes from Williams Alamu’s study sessions at the University of Ibadan. I also relied heavily on my friends and was never ashamed to ask questions when I didn’t understand something. I was fortunate to have classmates who were willing to help, including Lateef Basunu , Akinmusire Esther , Moyosoluwa Opesitian , Shukuroh Oladokun , Franklin David and Samuel Okoosi . Lateef, in particular, was incredibly patient and would spend as much time as necessary explaining difficult concepts to me. I also learnt that I assimilated information better in the morning. I’ve always been an early riser, usually awake by 5:30 a.m., so I preferred to sleep early rather than force myself to study through the night. I made an effort to plan my days around my priorities. Looking back, there wasn’t one extraordinary technique behind my academic performance. It was a combination of attending classes, studying early, taking notes, asking questions and understanding when I worked best. Williams Alamu combines virtual study sessions with printed Statistics notes during his undergraduate studies at the University of Ibadan. What did you have to sacrifice? Tell us about the social events, personal time, hobbies or even sleep you had to put aside to protect your CGPA. I think the biggest sacrifices I made were actually in my career. Outside academics, I’m a designer, working primarily in product design and web experiences. As I grew in the field, more opportunities started coming my way, including full-time and remote job offers. However, combining those responsibilities with my academic workload was difficult, especially because I had already set a goal for myself at university. I remember receiving an offer to join a company as its founding designer just as I was about to begin my final examinations. There was also another opportunity involving relocation abroad. Both were opportunities I genuinely wanted, but I had invested so much in my education that I didn’t want to compromise on the academic goal I had set for myself. I wouldn’t say I sacrificed much socially, as I’ve never been someone who attends a lot of parties. My hobbies were a different story. I enjoy video games, but I deliberately waited until after university to buy the Nintendo Switch I had always wanted because I knew it could become another distraction. Sleep was another thing I occasionally sacrificed during examinations. I remember staying awake for almost 36 hours while preparing for a Demography examination, and there were other nights when I studied until 2 or 3 a.m. Looking back, university was about deciding what deserved my attention at different points. I couldn’t give everything the same level of attention, and for those four years, my academics had to take priority. Williams Alamu takes a break during an overnight study session in his department at the University of Ibadan. How did you handle the toughest courses or departmental hurdles that usually break a student’s GPA? I’ve always believed that when you don’t understand something, there’s no point pretending otherwise. Whenever I struggled with a course or topic, I sought help from people who understood it better. One person who helped me tremendously was Lateef Basunu. I would visit him at his hostel for one-on-one tutorials, where he patiently explained difficult concepts and worked

item.title: My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos
item.description: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. item.dc:creator: Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé
item.content:encoded: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created. The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. We discussed the dangers of anachronism in contemporary fiction through the critique of a Nigerian novel and the anachronistic elements therein. She hammered on the importance of reading widely, beyond the mainstream, beyond the contemporary, across literary cultures and traditions. We must read widely so we can know exactly what we are writing in response to. The workshop’s goal is in its name. The rudiments of writing are well known to writers, but not so much those of editing. To polish a story to the best it can be. “ To develop the inner practice of being attentive to define and understand the times ” . Editing one’s own work can be difficult. The sentimental value we place on our words makes it hard to, as they say, “kill your darlings”, but it is a necessity for the beauty of a story to shine through. For the writing to be better, we simply “Gotta whack that guy!” as Molara Wood called out from her workshop material. The afternoon session was facilitated by the Liberian-American novelist, Wayétu Moore. Her session was on Speculative fiction/Magical Realism. Naturally, the question raised is the extent to which these categorisations apply to the works of those who write from cultures where the material and the mystical spheres are considered to be in constant interaction. Such that the happenings that seem magical to a Western mind are random stories one hears from neighbours, friends and family so often that they are as real as anything, and an immutable fact. Tales of cats that bring down house walls, of children who die and return again and again, of grandfathers who come back as babies, of birds dropping from the sky and transforming into old women. Wayétu Moore was in conversation with us about this. The most important eye-opener for me during this session was about plot and character building. The rules for writing nuanced characters are the same regardless of whether a story is speculative or realist. Writers tend to venerate certain characters as saints and demonise others with no redeemable qualities, such that they are a clear antithesis of the other. But human beings are not that way. A supposedly evil character can be a loving husband. A torturer can be a caring father when he returns home every night. This is the nature of humans, the nature of the characters we want to portray in stories. It has been said that reality doesn’t necessarily make sense, but fiction should. The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. “Forget technique… Write from here.” We all had one question on our tongues on the second day of the workshop: who wrote the assigned anonymised short story we were to discuss? It was a shocking story, quality-wise, and was written by one of the greats of 20th-century African Writing, we came to find out. A story that meanders and pulls up new surprises with every line. In a workshop with a focus on editing, it was the perfect case study for our facilitator to have us note not only its obvious flaws, but also its strengths. We learned even more about dialogue and voice, structural and contextual editing. The field was covered. Molara Wood wanted to get as much as possible done despite the short time we had together for the workshop. So we had to eat into our lunch breaks, quite literally. No complaints; there was so much to converse about. The sessions were interactive. We discussed each other’s writing samples, and then our works-in-progress in pairs, giving feedback on what we thought worked well, what didn’t. A way of putting into practice what we had spent hours learning during the workshop. One that was soon reaching its end. When Eghosa Imasuen and Anwuli Ojogwu of Narrative Landscape Press filled the room with their presence for the afternoon session, I knew it was going to be enjoyable. Eghosa Imasuen is a very jovial man, mixing English with Pidgin to land a point and make jokes. It felt as if he knew us all beforehand. The publishing industry in Nigeria has always fascinated me. What are contracts like? How well do books sell? These things are often shrouded in mystery. Eghosa spearheaded the session. Anwuli made her points where she thought necessary. Understanding the publishing process within a Nigerian publishing house like NLP was necessary for writers who, after fine-tuning stories or a novel, would seek out publishers. The session included tips on how to put together a publisher’s query for a manuscript, and the fine margins that can make a query sound professional and confident. “Be simple. Less is more,” Anwuli noted. You write a good story, rewrite, revise, edit, put together a pack of publishers’ queries and send it off with a hail of prayers. “Writers are the suppliers of stories,” Eghosa Imasuen explained. Publishers produce and sell them. It is looking at stories in the business sense, because publishing is a business, a precarious, courageous one. This was further highlighted when we got into the numbers of it all, information that I was glad to be privy to. The nature of p

item.title: The Beatz Awards 2026: Soso Soberekon Honoured with Special Recognition Award as May D and Shiiro Light Up 11th Edition
item.description: The 11th edition of The Beatz Awards, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at the Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, Onikan, Lagos, was a remarkable celebration of music, creativity, excellence and the exceptional talents working behind the scenes of the Nigerian music industry. Under the theme “Behind the Beat, Beyond the Beat,” this year’s ceremony brought together music professionals, industry stakeholders, producers, songwriters, DJs, engineers, media personalities and other key players to celebrate the creative minds whose contributions continue to shape the sound and business of African music. Soso Soberekon Receives Special Recognition Award One of the major highlights of the evening was the presentation of the Special Recognition Award to renowned music executive and industry figure, Soso Soberekon, in recognition of his remarkable contributions to the Nigerian music industry. From talent discovery and artist development to music promotion, business development and industry connections, Soso Soberekon’s influence and commitment to the growth of Nigerian entertainment continue to resonate across different sectors of the culture. The special recognition celebrates his role in creating opportunities, supporting talents and contributing to the development of the Nigerian music ecosystem. May D and Shiiro Deliver Electrifying Performances The ceremony also featured captivating musical performances, with award-winning singer May D delivering an electrifying performance that got the audience on their feet, while producer and songwriter Shiiro equally thrilled guests with an impressive performance, showcasing the creativity and musical excellence that The Beatz Awards continues to celebrate. Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge: Kevwe Praise Emerges Winner Another major highlight of the 11th edition was the highly anticipated Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge, an initiative designed to discover, nurture and provide opportunities for emerging music producers. The competition provided a platform for talented producers who participated in the Beatz to Banger 2.0 training programme to showcase their creativity, technical abilities and music production skills before an audience of industry professionals. Following an intense competition among the final five contestants, Kevwe Praise emerged as the ultimate winner, earning the coveted title and a cash prize of ₦1.5 million. The winner’s cash cheque was presented by Princess Damilola Sonayon-James , APC Deputy Governorship Aspirant, alongside the Chief Executive Officer of The Beatz Awards, Elijah John . The moment marked a significant milestone for the winning producer and reinforced The Beatz Awards’ commitment to creating tangible opportunities for emerging talents beyond recognition and celebration. item.title: Temi Nkem’s Oversized Braided Updo Is the Hairstyle Inspiration We Needed
item.description: Big Brother Naija 2026 winner Temi Nkem pairs a structured matte-gold leather corset and black velvet skirt with an architectural braided updo. If your next braid appointment has you thinking beyond the usual ponytail or bun, Temi Nkem has an idea you might want to take to your hairstylist. The Big Brother Naija 2026 winner wore her thick braids in a high, sculptural updo, with oversized loops arranged into a crown. She paired it with a gold-and-black look, complete with metallic beauty details and contrasting textures. Rather than letting her thick braids fall down her back, Temi has gathered them into a sleek, high updo, building them into an oversized crown of interlocking loops. The result is sculptural, full of volume and beautifully structured. It’s also a great example of how to style thick braids when you want a fresh way to wear them for an event. Pulling the hair up keeps the face open, while the loops create plenty of interest around the crown. And with the base kept sleek, the hairstyle gets to take centre stage without feeling too busy. Temi Nkem accents her sleek looped braid updo with metallic gold-leaf detailing, brow crystal, and glossy nude lips. Then there are the beauty details. Temi goes for smoky brown eyeshadow, full lashes and a glossy nude lip outlined in brown, keeping the makeup warm and complementary to the outfit. A little gold takes things further: there’s a tiny cross-shaped crystal between her brows, three vertical micro-beads on her chin, hammered circular gold earrings and flecks of metallic gold leaf tracing the side of her face, from her left temple down to her collarbone. It’s an unexpected beauty detail, and one that ties in beautifully with the colours of her outfit. Temi Nkem shows how to style thick braids into a sculptural crown paired with a gold-and-black corset gown. Now, about that gown! Temi shows how to wear gold and black with ease, starting with a structured matte-gold leather corset bodice. It features vertical seam boning, a deep V-plunge neckline and a sharply defined V-shaped basque waist. Below it, a fitted black velvet skirt brings a different texture into the look, while matching off-the-shoulder velvet arm bands complete the silhouette. The contrast between the gold leather and plush black velvet is what makes the combination work so well. Rather than having both colours compete for attention, the matte gold adds warmth and the black velvet gives the outfit balance. So, if thick braids are next on your salon mood board, you might want to save Temi’s updo. And if you’re planning a gold-and-black outfit, her mix of leather and velvet is another styling idea worth keeping. item.title: Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours
item.description: My name is Enoch Adeagbo. In 2021, at the age of 14, I was refused admission because I was too young. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14. On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at 19, I will graduate from ACU with First Class Honours in Civil Engineering, having earned a CGPA of 4.79 out of 5.00, as the second-best student in my department and the third-best student in the Faculty of Engineering. If I had given up and not applied to another school, I might not be here today sharing my journey. Where it all began As a child, I often accompanied my father to construction sites. I enjoyed watching structures take shape from foundation stage to completion. My interest in how buildings were designed and constructed gradually developed into a desire to become an engineer. At 14, however, I was considerably younger than most of my course mates. People frequently reminded me of my age, and I had to adjust. I learnt to focus on my studies, take part in university activities and make the most of the opportunity I had been given. In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent. The C that taught me something But being interested in a course does not necessarily mean you’d understand it completely. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was surprised because I had been confident in my knowledge of the course. That experience made me reflect on my approach to studying. I became more deliberate about understanding concepts rather than simply assuming I had mastered them. Studying with a group and teaching my coursemates also became valuable. Explaining a topic to someone else also helped me understand the course more. More than lectures Beyond the classroom, I served as the Academic Officer of the Nigerian Universities Engineering Students’ Association (NUESA), ACU Chapter, for the 2025/2026 session. I also served as an Assistant Class Representative and was involved in chapel activities as a chapel worker. My faith in God has played an important role throughout my university journey. It shaped my discipline, decisions and priorities, and helped me remain intentional about my responsibilities. I am grateful to my parents, who made sure I did not have to worry about finances while pursuing my education. Their support allowed me to concentrate on my studies and other responsibilities without the additional burden of financial concerns.
